## Statement

Assume AC. Fix $0<\gamma\le1$. Let $1\le d\le4$, $s>0$, $B>0$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_m,Z$ be independent centered random vectors in $\mathbb R^d$, where $m\ge0$, $|X_j|\le B$ almost surely, and $Z\sim N_d(0,G)$. Suppose $S=Z+\sum_jX_j$ has covariance $sI_d$ and $G\ge\gamma sI_d$ in quadratic form order. There is an absolute constant $C_0\ge1$ such that, with $\tau=C_0B$, the logarithmic moment generating function
$$K(z)=\log\mathbb E e^{z\cdot S},\qquad K(0)=0,$$
has a single analytic branch on the complex Euclidean ball $\tau|z|<1$, and
$$|\partial_u\partial_v^2K(z)|\le\tau s|u||v|^2\qquad(u,v\in\mathbb R^d,\ \tau|z|<1).$$
Here $z\cdot S$ uses the complex bilinear dot product and $|z|^2=\sum_i|z_i|^2$. Every real exponential tilt $\mathbb P_h(d\omega)=e^{h\cdot S-K(h)}\mathbb P(d\omega)$ is defined, and its characteristic function satisfies
$$|\varphi_h(t)|:=|\mathbb E_h e^{it\cdot S}|\le e^{-\gamma s|t|^2/2}\qquad(t,h\in\mathbb R^d),$$
where $K(h)=\log\mathbb E e^{h\cdot S}$ for real $h$, also outside the analytic ball. Put $\kappa=\tau/\sqrt s$. For every fixed $a>0$ and integer $N\ge1$ there is a finite $C_{a,N,\gamma}$, uniform in $1\le d\le4$, such that, if $0<\kappa\le1$,
$$(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{|t|\ge a/\tau}|\varphi_h(t)|\,dt\le C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^Ns^{-d/2},$$
$$(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{|t|\ge a/\tau}|t\cdot v||\varphi_h(t)|\,dt\le C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^N|v|s^{-(d+1)/2}.$$
All assertions hold with the same $C_0$, $B$, $s$, and $\gamma$ for $AS$, where $A$ is any real $k\times d$ matrix with $1\le k\le d$ and $AA^T=I_k$. This includes every coordinate prefix, every orthogonal change of coordinates, and their compositions. In particular it covers the normalized joint sum and difference of two independent children by applying the assertion in their joint dimension, provided that dimension is at most four and the joint input satisfies the stated covariance assumptions.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses of the Statement; all vector norms are Euclidean, and all matrix orders are orders of real quadratic forms.

[F1] Finite products of integrable functions of independent variables factor in expectation. [[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]].

[F2] Dominated convergence interchanges limits and integrals under an integrable absolute majorant. [[thm-dominated-convergence]].

[F3] Absolute Fubini and nonnegative Tonelli apply to the probability and Lebesgue integrals below. [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]].

[F4] A positive definite Gaussian law has density $q_G(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det G)^{-1/2}e^{-x^TG^{-1}x/2}$ and a Gaussian with covariance $G$ has characteristic function $e^{-t^TGt/2}$. [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]], [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-multivariate-normal-law]].

[F6] Locally uniformly convergent holomorphic series are holomorphic, the one-variable identity theorem extends equality from a real interval, and linear changes of Lebesgue variables have their determinant Jacobian. [[cor-locally-uniformly-convergent-holomorphic-series]], [[thm-identity-theorem-holomorphic-functions]], [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]].

[F5] Euclidean Cauchy–Schwarz bounds $|u\cdot x|\le|u||x|$, and its integral version follows by integrating $(f-cg)^2\ge0$ and minimizing in real $c$. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]].

[A1] AC is assumed and inherited by the Gaussian suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

## Proof

1.1 Fix one centered bounded summand $X$ with covariance $D$, and put $M(z)=\mathbb E e^{z\cdot X}$. Its exponential series converges uniformly on every bounded complex set because $|X|\le B$, and the expectation of its absolute series is bounded by $e^{B|z|}$; thus termwise integration defines an entire function and its derivatives are the expectations of the corresponding polynomial factors times the exponential. Fix an absolute $b>0$ with $e^b-1\le1/2$. If $B|z|<b$, then $|M(z)-1|\le e^{B|z|}-1\le1/2$, so the convergent power series for $\log(1+(M(z)-1))$ supplies a single analytic logarithm vanishing at zero. [given, F2, F5, F6]

1.2 On this ball, writing subscripts for directional derivatives, the bounds $|e^{z\cdot X}|\le e^b$, $|u\cdot X|\le B|u|$, and $\mathbb E(v\cdot X)^2=v^TDv$ give $|M_u|\le e^bB|u|$, $|M_v|\le e^b\sqrt{v^TDv}$, $|M_{vv}|\le e^bv^TDv$, $|M_{uv}|\le e^bB|u|\sqrt{v^TDv}$, and $|M_{uvv}|\le e^bB|u|v^TDv$. These inequalities also hold when $D$ is singular: a direction with zero second moment has $v\cdot X=0$ almost surely. [step 1.1, F5]

1.3 Direct differentiation gives $(\log M)_{uvv}=M_{uvv}/M-(M_uM_{vv}+2M_vM_{uv})/M^2+2M_uM_v^2/M^3$. Since $|M|\ge1/2$, step 1.2 bounds this by $CB|u|v^TDv$ for one absolute finite $C$. Choose $C_0$ so that $C_0\ge C$ and $1/C_0<b$, and set $\tau=C_0B$. Each bounded summand therefore has the asserted derivative bound on $\tau|z|<1$, using its own covariance. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra, choose]

2.1 Completing the square in the density in [F4] shows $\mathbb E e^{h\cdot Z}=e^{h^TGh/2}$ for real $h$ and that its real tilt is $N_d(Gh,G)$. The same integral for complex $z$ converges absolutely on bounded complex sets: $e^{\operatorname{Re}(z)\cdot x}$ times the Gaussian density is a constant times a translated Gaussian density, which dominates its polynomial derivatives on smaller bounded sets. Its exponential series or differentiated integral therefore gives an entire function, and the real identity extends to complex arguments. To justify that last extension without a several-variable identity theorem, fix all but the first coordinate real and apply the one-variable identity theorem, then successively free each remaining coordinate. Thus the Gaussian cumulant is $z^TGz/2$ and has zero third derivative. [F2, F4, F6, algebra]

2.2 By independence [F1], the moment generating function of $S$ is the product of the factors in steps 1.1 and 2.1. On $\tau|z|<1$, its logarithm is the sum of the analytic logarithms just constructed, with value zero at zero. Since the covariances add and $\sum_j\operatorname{cov}(X_j)\le sI_d$, summing step 1.3 gives $|K_{uvv}(z)|\le\tau|u|\sum_jv^T\operatorname{cov}(X_j)v\le\tau s|u||v|^2$. This proves the analytic assertion, including the empty bounded sum. [step 1.3, step 2.1, F1, algebra]

3.1 Every real tilt exists because all bounded-summand moment generating functions and the Gaussian one are finite and strictly positive. Its density with respect to the original independent joint law factors as the product of the separately normalized tilt densities. Hence those summands remain independent under the tilt. Step 2.1 shows that the Gaussian factor retains covariance $G$, while each other factor has a characteristic function of modulus at most one because $|e^{it\cdot X_j}|=1$. Factorization and [F4] therefore give $|\varphi_h(t)|\le e^{-t^TGt/2}\le e^{-\gamma s|t|^2/2}$ for every real $h,t$. [step 2.1, F1, F4]

3.2 Substitute $u=\sqrt s\,t$ in each requested tail integral, using the constant Jacobian $s^{-d/2}$. For $|u|\ge a/\kappa$, $e^{-\gamma|u|^2/2}\le e^{-\gamma a^2/(4\kappa^2)}e^{-\gamma|u|^2/4}$. For every fixed $N$, the function $z\mapsto z^Ne^{-\gamma a^2z^2/4}$ is bounded on $z\ge1$ by differentiation, so the extracted exponential is at most $C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^N$. The integral of $e^{-\gamma|u|^2/4}$ is finite by the normal density normalization in [F4]; its product with $|u|$ is integrable as well, since $|u|e^{-\gamma|u|^2/8}$ is bounded and the remaining Gaussian is integrable. Using $|u\cdot v|\le|u||v|$ gives the two tail bounds, with an additional $s^{-1/2}|v|$ in the weighted bound. Taking the maximum of these constants over $d=1,2,3,4$ makes them uniform. [step 3.1, F3, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

4.1 If $AA^T=I_k$, the operator norm of $A$ is one: $A^T$ is an isometry and $|Ax|=\sup_{|v|=1}|v\cdot Ax|\le|x|$ by [F5]. Thus $AX_j$ remains bounded by $B$ and centered, its sum has covariance $sAA^T=sI_k$, and $AZ$ is Gaussian with covariance $AGA^T\ge\gamma sI_k$ by [F4]. Independence is preserved by applying measurable maps separately. All earlier steps therefore apply to $AS$ with the same $C_0$. The map $(x,y)\mapsto((x+y)/\sqrt2,(x-y)/\sqrt2)$ is orthogonal because it preserves $|x|^2+|y|^2$ by expansion; consequently its coordinate prefixes have the required row isometry property. This proves all assertions. [step 2.2, step 3.1, step 3.2, F4, F5, algebra] ∎

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open and let $g_j:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic. Suppose the sequence of partial sums of $\sum_{j\ge0}g_j$ converges locally uniformly to $g$. Then $g$ is holomorphic, and for every natural $k$,

$$g^{(k)}=\sum_{j\ge0}g_j^{(k)},$$

where the derivative series converges locally uniformly.

If two holomorphic functions on a complex domain agree on a set with an accumulation point in the domain, then they agree everywhere on the domain.

Precisely, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a complex domain ([[def-complex-domain]]), let $f,g:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose that some $a\in\Omega$ is an accumulation point of $\{z\in\Omega:f(z)=g(z)\}$. Then $f=g$ on $\Omega$. The requirement $a\in\Omega$ is essential.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

## Statement

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[lem-gaussian-anchored-sums-have-cumulant-and-fourier-bounds]], with $1\le d\le4$, fixed $\gamma>0$, $\tau=C_0B$, $\kappa=\tau/\sqrt s$, and logarithmic moment generating function $K$. Let $p_h$ denote the density of $S$ under the real exponential tilt with parameter $h$. Every such density exists, is continuously differentiable and strictly positive, and
$$\sup_y p_h(y)\le(2\pi\gamma s)^{-d/2}\qquad(h\in\mathbb R^d).$$
There are constants $c_\gamma>0$, $C_\gamma<\infty$, independent of $d,s,B,m$ and the summand laws, with the following property. If $\kappa\le c_\gamma$ and $\tau|h|\le1/8$, put $\mu_h=\mathbb E_hS$ and $D_h=\operatorname{cov}_h(S)$. Then
$$\tfrac78sI_d\le D_h\le\tfrac98sI_d.$$
For $x\in\mathbb R^d$ put $r=|D_h^{-1/2}x|$ and let $q_{D_h}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det D_h)^{-1/2}e^{-r^2/2}$. Whenever $\kappa r\le c_\gamma$,
$$\left|\log\frac{p_h(\mu_h+x)}{q_{D_h}(x)}\right|\le C_\gamma\kappa(1+r^3).$$
For $r\ge7$ in the same region,
$$\left.\frac{d}{dt}\log p_h(\mu_h+x+tx)\right|_{t=0}\le-\tfrac12r^2.$$
These assertions apply separately to every row isometry image in the supplier, including every required coordinate prefix and normalized joint child sum and difference. Their tilt parameter and covariance are taken in that image's own coordinates.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses of the Statement. The inverse square root of a positive definite matrix is its symmetric positive inverse square root, and directional derivatives at a point always keep the chosen exponential tilt fixed.

[F1] The bounded and Gaussian sum has an analytic cumulant with $|K_{uvv}(z)|\le\tau s|u||v|^2$ on $\tau|z|<1$. Under every real tilt its Gaussian component remains independent with covariance $G\ge\gamma sI_d$, its characteristic function has modulus at most $e^{-\gamma s|t|^2/2}$, and its Fourier tails, with or without one linear frequency factor, decay faster than any fixed power of $\kappa$. The same holds for every row isometry image. [[lem-gaussian-anchored-sums-have-cumulant-and-fourier-bounds]].

[F2] Positive definite Gaussian densities have the displayed quadratic form and total mass one; their characteristic functions are the matching Gaussian exponentials. [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]], [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-multivariate-normal-law]].

[F3] Fubini, Tonelli and dominated convergence license absolutely integrable interchanges and dominated differentiation. [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]].

[F4] Real symmetric matrices have orthonormal eigenbases; linear changes of Lebesgue variables multiply by the absolute determinant. [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]], [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]].

## Proof

1.1 Under any real tilt, write $S=Y+Z_h$, where the two terms are independent and $Z_h$ is Gaussian of covariance $G$ by [F1]. Tonelli and translation of the Gaussian density show that $p_h(y)=\mathbb E_hq_G(y-Y-\mathbb E_hZ_h)$ is a probability density. It is strictly positive because its integrand is strictly positive, and is bounded by $(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det G)^{-1/2}\le(2\pi\gamma s)^{-d/2}$. The Gaussian density and each of its first derivatives are bounded and continuous, so dominated convergence gives continuous first derivatives of this convolution. This proves the global assertions without a general vector inversion theorem. [F1, F2, F3, F4]

1.2 We will also need its Fourier formula. Integrating the density of $N_d(0,G^{-1})$ against the character $e^{-it\cdot y}$ and using its characteristic function in [F2] gives $q_G(y)=(2\pi)^{-d}\int e^{-it\cdot y}e^{-t^TGt/2}\,dt$. The constants follow directly by inserting that density and multiplying by $(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det G)^{-1/2}$. Insert this formula in step 1.1 and use absolute Fubini, dominated by the integrable Gaussian $e^{-t^TGt/2}$. Thus $p_h(y)=(2\pi)^{-d}\int e^{-it\cdot y}\varphi_h(t)\,dt$, and its derivative in direction $v$ is the same integral with factor $-i(t\cdot v)$. This differentiation is dominated because $|t\cdot v|e^{-\gamma s|t|^2/2}$ is integrable by [F1]. Centering or making an invertible linear change of coordinates gives the identical formulas for those transformed densities. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, F4]

2.1 Exponential moment differentiation identifies $K'(h)$ and $K''(h)$ with the tilted mean and covariance, respectively. To justify the differentiation, the bounded summands permit every polynomial factor, and the Gaussian square completion in [F1] makes all its polynomial moments integrable even after a slightly stronger real exponential; dominated convergence applies. For real $u,v,w$, polarization of the symmetric complex valued form $Q(v,w)=K_{uvw}(z)$ gives $|Q(v,w)|\le\tau s|u||v||w|$: apply $4Q(v,w)=Q(v+w,v+w)-Q(v-w,v-w)$ after replacing $v,w$ by $av,a^{-1}w$, and minimize the resulting bound $\tau s|u|(a^2|v|^2+a^{-2}|w|^2)/2$ over $a>0$. Integrating $K'''$ on the real segment from zero to $h$ therefore gives $\|K''(h)-sI\|\le\tau s|h|$. Hence $7sI/8\le D_h\le9sI/8$ for $\tau|h|\le1/8$. [F1, F3, F5, algebra]

2.2 Fix this $h$ and center its law. Its cumulant is $K_h(z)=K(h+z)-K(h)-z\cdot\mu_h$. On $2\tau|z|<1$ the original analytic ball still contains $h+z$, since $\tau|h+z|<5/8$. Its third derivative is bounded by $\tau s|u||v|^2\le2\tau|u|v^TD_hv$. Whiten by $D_h^{-1/2}$, writing $W=D_h^{-1/2}(S-\mu_h)$ under this tilt and $L(a)=K_h(D_h^{-1/2}a)$. Then $L(0)=0$, $L'(0)=0$, $L''(0)=I$, and, with $\lambda=2\tau/\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(D_h)}\le3\kappa$, it is analytic on $\lambda|a|<1$ and satisfies $|L_{uvv}(a)|\le\lambda|u||v|^2$. The centered Gaussian component of $W$ has covariance at least $(8\gamma/9)I$. Its covariance remains unchanged under every further real tilt; consequently all such tilted characteristic functions have modulus at most $e^{-(4\gamma/9)|t|^2}$. [step 2.1, F1, F4, algebra]

3.1 Polarization as in step 2.1 and integration along $ta$, $0\le t\le1$, give $\|L''(a)-I\|\le\lambda|a|$, $|L'(a)-a|\le\lambda|a|^2/2$, and $|L(a)-|a|^2/2|\le\lambda|a|^3/6$ for real $a$ in the ball. For real $t$ the same last estimate along the complex segment $ist$ gives $L(it)=-|t|^2/2+R(t)$ with $|R(t)|\le\lambda|t|^3/6$: this uses only the real direction $t$ in each derivative and the factors $i^3$ from the segment parameter. [step 2.2, F5, algebra]

3.2 Put $b=D_h^{-1/2}x$, $r=|b|$. If $\lambda r\le1/16$, the map $T(a)=b-(L'(a)-a)$ sends the closed ball $|a|\le2r$ into itself by step 3.1, and its Lipschitz constant there is at most $2\lambda r\le1/8$. Starting at zero, its iterates are Cauchy since consecutive distances decrease geometrically; their limit exists by [F6], lies in the closed ball, and is a fixed point by continuity. Call it $a$. It satisfies $L'(a)=b$, $|a|\le2r$, and $|a-b|\le2\lambda r^2$. For $r=0$ take $a=0$. Thus no unproved global inverse assertion is needed for the saddlepoint. [step 3.1, F5, F6, construct]

3.3 Tilt $W$ further by the fixed parameter $a$. Its mean is $b$ and covariance $A=L''(a)$. Put $\epsilon=\lambda|a|\le2\lambda r$; step 3.1 gives $(1-\epsilon)I\le A\le(1+\epsilon)I$. Its cumulant centered at $b$ has third derivative bounded by a fixed multiple of $\lambda|u||v|^2$ on a complex ball of radius $c/\lambda$, because $a$ lies in the interior of the original analytic ball by step 3.2. Its characteristic modulus on all real frequencies is bounded by the same Gaussian $e^{-(4\gamma/9)|t|^2}$ from step 2.2. In what follows reduce the final constant $c_\gamma$ so that $\epsilon\le1/100$ and all these interior margins hold. [step 2.2, step 3.1, step 3.2, choose]

4.1 Let $\psi(t)$ be that last centered characteristic function and let $g_A=(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det A)^{-1/2}$. For $|t|\le a_0/\lambda$, with a sufficiently small fixed $a_0>0$, the integrated third derivative estimate gives $\log\psi(t)=-t^TAt/2+E(t)$, $|E(t)|\le C\lambda|t|^3$, and $\operatorname{Re}\log\psi(t)\le-c|t|^2$. The elementary identity $e^z-e^w=(z-w)\int_0^1e^{(1-u)w+uz}\,du$ therefore gives $|\psi(t)-e^{-t^TAt/2}|\le C\lambda|t|^3e^{-c|t|^2}$ there. Its integral, and its integral after multiplication by $|t\cdot v|$, are bounded by $C\lambda$ and $C\lambda|v|$, respectively. To check the integrability explicitly, $|t|^je^{-c|t|^2/2}$ is bounded for each fixed $j$, by differentiation in $|t|$, and the remaining Gaussian is integrable by [F2]. Constants are uniform over $d\le4$ and $A$ in the displayed neighborhood of $I$. [step 3.3, F2, F5, algebra]

4.2 Outside the ball of step 4.1, both $\psi$ and the Gaussian comparator have unweighted integral $O_\gamma(\lambda^2)$ and weighted integral $O_\gamma(\lambda^2|v|)$. Indeed their global bounds are $e^{-c_\gamma|t|^2}$; extract $e^{-c_\gamma a_0^2/(2\lambda^2)}$ and integrate the remaining Gaussian, also with $|t\cdot v|$. The extracted exponential is smaller than any prescribed fixed power of $\lambda$ because $z^je^{-cz^2}$ is bounded. This is the same direct Gaussian tail argument as [F1], and uses no smoothness condition on a lattice law. Combining this with step 4.1 and the Fourier formula of step 1.2 gives, for the density $f_a$ of the further tilted $W$,
$$|f_a(b)-g_A|\le C_\gamma\lambda,\qquad \sup_y|\partial_v f_a(y)|\le\left(\sqrt{2/\pi}\,g_A\sqrt{v^TA^{-1}v}+C_\gamma\lambda|v|\right).$$
The Gaussian integral in the derivative bound is exact: transform by $A^{1/2}$ and rotate $A^{-1/2}v$ onto the first coordinate; the standard Gaussian first absolute moment is $\sqrt{2/\pi}$, from $\int_0^\infty t e^{-t^2/2}dt=1$. [step 1.2, step 4.1, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

5.1 The eigenvalue bounds in step 3.3 give $|\log\det A|\le C d\epsilon$ because $|\log(1+u)|\le2|u|$ for $|u|\le1/2$, by integrating $(1+u)^{-1}$. Thus $g_A$ is bounded above and away from zero, uniformly, and $\log(g_A/(2\pi)^{-d/2})=O(\lambda r)$. Step 4.2 and $|\log(1+u)|\le2|u|$ imply $f_a(b)>0$ and
$$\log\frac{f_a(b)}{(2\pi)^{-d/2}}=O_\gamma(\lambda(1+r)).$$

manifest_row.statement:
Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[lem-gaussian-anchored-sums-have-cumulant-and-fourier-bounds]], with $1\le d\le4$, fixed $\gamma>0$, $\tau=C_0B$, $\kappa=\tau/\sqrt s$, and logarithmic moment generating function $K$. Let $p_h$ denote the density of $S$ under the real exponential tilt with parameter $h$. Every such density exists, is continuously differentiable and strictly positive, and
$$\sup_y p_h(y)\le(2\pi\gamma s)^{-d/2}\qquad(h\in\mathbb R^d).$$
There are constants $c_\gamma>0$, $C_\gamma<\infty$, independent of $d,s,B,m$ and the summand laws, with the following property. If $\kappa\le c_\gamma$ and $\tau|h|\le1/8$, put $\mu_h=\mathbb E_hS$ and $D_h=\operatorname{cov}_h(S)$. Then
$$\tfrac78sI_d\le D_h\le\tfrac98sI_d.$$
For $x\in\mathbb R^d$ put $r=|D_h^{-1/2}x|$ and let $q_{D_h}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det D_h)^{-1/2}e^{-r^2/2}$. Whenever $\kappa r\le c_\gamma$,
$$\left|\log\frac{p_h(\mu_h+x)}{q_{D_h}(x)}\right|\le C_\gamma\kappa(1+r^3).$$
For $r\ge7$ in the same region,
$$\left.\frac{d}{dt}\log p_h(\mu_h+x+tx)\right|_{t=0}\le-\tfrac12r^2.$$
These assertions apply separately to every row isometry image in the supplier, including every required coordinate prefix and normalized joint child sum and difference. Their tilt parameter and covariance are taken in that image's own coordinates.

Assume AC. Fix $0<\gamma\le1$. Let $1\le d\le4$, $s>0$, $B>0$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_m,Z$ be independent centered random vectors in $\mathbb R^d$, where $m\ge0$, $|X_j|\le B$ almost surely, and $Z\sim N_d(0,G)$. Suppose $S=Z+\sum_jX_j$ has covariance $sI_d$ and $G\ge\gamma sI_d$ in quadratic form order. There is an absolute constant $C_0\ge1$ such that, with $\tau=C_0B$, the logarithmic moment generating function
$$K(z)=\log\mathbb E e^{z\cdot S},\qquad K(0)=0,$$
has a single analytic branch on the complex Euclidean ball $\tau|z|<1$, and
$$|\partial_u\partial_v^2K(z)|\le\tau s|u||v|^2\qquad(u,v\in\mathbb R^d,\ \tau|z|<1).$$
Here $z\cdot S$ uses the complex bilinear dot product and $|z|^2=\sum_i|z_i|^2$. Every real exponential tilt $\mathbb P_h(d\omega)=e^{h\cdot S-K(h)}\mathbb P(d\omega)$ is defined, and its characteristic function satisfies
$$|\varphi_h(t)|:=|\mathbb E_h e^{it\cdot S}|\le e^{-\gamma s|t|^2/2}\qquad(t,h\in\mathbb R^d),$$
where $K(h)=\log\mathbb E e^{h\cdot S}$ for real $h$, also outside the analytic ball. Put $\kappa=\tau/\sqrt s$. For every fixed $a>0$ and integer $N\ge1$ there is a finite $C_{a,N,\gamma}$, uniform in $1\le d\le4$, such that, if $0<\kappa\le1$,
$$(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{|t|\ge a/\tau}|\varphi_h(t)|\,dt\le C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^Ns^{-d/2},$$
$$(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{|t|\ge a/\tau}|t\cdot v||\varphi_h(t)|\,dt\le C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^N|v|s^{-(d+1)/2}.$$
All assertions hold with the same $C_0$, $B$, $s$, and $\gamma$ for $AS$, where $A$ is any real $k\times d$ matrix with $1\le k\le d$ and $AA^T=I_k$. This includes every coordinate prefix, every orthogonal change of coordinates, and their compositions. In particular it covers the normalized joint sum and difference of two independent children by applying the assertion in their joint dimension, provided that dimension is at most four and the joint input satisfies the stated covariance assumptions.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Its covariance remains unchanged under every further real tilt; consequently all such tilted characteristic functions have modulus at most $e^{-(4\gamma/9)|t|^2}$.

Polarization as in step 2.1 and integration along $ta$, $0\le t\le1$, give $\|L''(a)-I\|\le\lambda|a|$, $|L'(a)-a|\le\lambda|a|^2/2$, and $|L(a)-|a|^2/2|\le\lambda|a|^3/6$ for real $a$ in the ball. For real $t$ the same last estimate along the complex segment $ist$ gives $L(it)=-|t|^2/2+R(t)$ with $|R(t)|\le\lambda|t|^3/6$: this uses only the real direction $t$ in each derivative and the factors $i^3$ from the segment parameter.

Put $b=D_h^{-1/2}x$, $r=|b|$. If $\lambda r\le1/16$, the map $T(a)=b-(L'(a)-a)$ sends the closed ball $|a|\le2r$ into itself by step 3.1, and its Lipschitz constant there is at most $2\lambda r\le1/8$. Starting at zero, its iterates are Cauchy since consecutive distances decrease geometrically; their limit exists by [F6], lies in the closed ball, and is a fixed point by continuity. Call it $a$. It satisfies $L'(a)=b$, $|a|\le2r$, and $|a-b|\le2\lambda r^2$. For $r=0$ take $a=0$. Thus no unproved global inverse assertion is needed for the saddlepoint.

Tilt $W$ further by the fixed parameter $a$. Its mean is $b$ and covariance $A=L''(a)$. Put $\epsilon=\lambda|a|\le2\lambda r$; step 3.1 gives $(1-\epsilon)I\le A\le(1+\epsilon)I$. Its cumulant centered at $b$ has third derivative bounded by a fixed multiple of $\lambda|u||v|^2$ on a complex ball of radius $c/\lambda$, because $a$ lies in the interior of the original analytic ball by step 3.2. Its characteristic modulus on all real frequencies is bounded by the same Gaussian $e^{-(4\gamma/9)|t|^2}$ from step 2.2. In what follows reduce the final constant $c_\gamma$ so that $\epsilon\le1/100$ and all these interior margins hold.

Let $\psi(t)$ be that last centered characteristic function and let $g_A=(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det A)^{-1/2}$. For $|t|\le a_0/\lambda$, with a sufficiently small fixed $a_0>0$, the integrated third derivative estimate gives $\log\psi(t)=-t^TAt/2+E(t)$, $|E(t)|\le C\lambda|t|^3$, and $\operatorname{Re}\log\psi(t)\le-c|t|^2$. The elementary identity $e^z-e^w=(z-w)\int_0^1e^{(1-u)w+uz}\,du$ therefore gives $|\psi(t)-e^{-t^TAt/2}|\le C\lambda|t|^3e^{-c|t|^2}$ there. Its integral, and its integral after multiplication by $|t\cdot v|$, are bounded by $C\lambda$ and $C\lambda|v|$, respectively. To check the integrability explicitly, $|t|^je^{-c|t|^2/2}$ is bounded for each fixed $j$, by differentiation in $|t|$, and the remaining Gaussian is integrable by [F2]. Constants are uniform over $d\le4$ and $A$ in the displayed neighborhood of $I$.

Outside the ball of step 4.1, both $\psi$ and the Gaussian comparator have unweighted integral $O_\gamma(\lambda^2)$ and weighted integral $O_\gamma(\lambda^2|v|)$. Indeed their global bounds are $e^{-c_\gamma|t|^2}$; extract $e^{-c_\gamma a_0^2/(2\lambda^2)}$ and integrate the remaining Gaussian, also with $|t\cdot v|$. The extracted exponential is smaller than any prescribed fixed power of $\lambda$ because $z^je^{-cz^2}$ is bounded. This is the same direct Gaussian tail argument as [F1], and uses no smoothness condition on a lattice law. Combining this with step 4.1 and the Fourier formula of step 1.2 gives, for the density $f_a$ of the further tilted $W$,
$$|f_a(b)-g_A|\le C_\gamma\lambda,\qquad \sup_y|\partial_v f_a(y)|\le\left(\sqrt{2/\pi}\,g_A\sqrt{v^TA^{-1}v}+C_\gamma\lambda|v|\right).$$
The Gaussian integral in the derivative bound is exact: transform by $A^{1/2}$ and rotate $A^{-1/2}v$ onto the first coordinate; the standard Gaussian first absolute moment is $\sqrt{2/\pi}$, from $\int_0^\infty t e^{-t^2/2}dt=1$.

The eigenvalue bounds in step 3.3 give $|\log\det A|\le C d\epsilon$ because $|\log(1+u)|\le2|u|$ for $|u|\le1/2$, by integrating $(1+u)^{-1}$. Thus $g_A$ is bounded above and away from zero, uniformly, and $\log(g_A/(2\pi)^{-d/2})=O(\lambda r)$. Step 4.2 and $|\log(1+u)|\le2|u|$ imply $f_a(b)>0$ and
$$\log\frac{f_a(b)}{(2\pi)^{-d/2}}=O_\gamma(\lambda(1+r)).$$
We choose $c_\gamma$ small enough that all relative errors used here are at most $1/100$.

The exact exponential tilt density identity is $f(y)=f_a(y)e^{L(a)-a\cdot y}$, where $f$ is the original density of $W$. It initially follows almost everywhere from the definition of the tilt; both sides are continuous by step 1.1, so it holds everywhere, since a continuous nonzero difference would be nonzero on a ball of positive Lebesgue measure. Step 3.1 and $|a-b|\le2\lambda r^2$ give
$$L(a)-a\cdot b=-r^2/2+O(\lambda r^3).$$
Indeed $|a|^2/2-a\cdot b=-|b|^2/2+|a-b|^2/2$, whose error is $O(\lambda^2r^4)=O(\lambda r^3)$ because $\lambda r$ is small. Combining this identity with step 5.1 proves $|\log(f(b)/q_I(b))|\le C_\gamma\lambda(1+r^3)$. The constant Jacobian for whitening cancels in the density ratio, and $\lambda\le3\kappa$ gives the stated moderate deviation bound.

Differentiate the exact identity in step 5.2 in direction $b$ at $y=b$, keeping $a$ fixed. It gives $\partial_b\log f(b)=(\partial_bf_a(b))/f_a(b)-a\cdot b$. By step 4.2, step 5.1, and $A=I+O(\lambda r)$, reduce $c_\gamma$ further so that $|\partial_bf_a(b)|/f_a(b)\le1.4r$; this is possible because its limiting coefficient is $\sqrt{2/\pi}<1$, the error is $O_\gamma(\lambda)$, and $A$ tends uniformly to $I$ as $\lambda r\to0$. Also step 3.2 gives $a\cdot b\ge r^2-2\lambda r^3\ge.99r^2$ after the same reduction. Hence $\partial_b\log f(b)\le1.4r-.99r^2\le-r^2/2$ for $r\ge7$. Whitening identifies this derivative with the derivative in direction $x$ in the Statement.

There are only finitely many smallness requirements above: bounds on $\kappa$, $\lambda r$, $\epsilon$, and fixed multiples depending only on $\gamma$ of $\lambda$. Since $\lambda\le3\kappa$, one sufficiently small positive $c_\gamma$ enforces all of them whenever $\kappa\le c_\gamma$ and $\kappa r\le c_\gamma$. All constants are uniform over dimensions one through four. Apply the same argument to a row isometry image using [F1]; its Gaussian component retains the same covariance lower bound, and every step applies in its own coordinates. This proves the remaining assertions.

## Statement

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[lem-gaussian-anchored-sums-have-cumulant-and-fourier-bounds]]: $S=Z+\sum_{i=1}^mX_i\in\mathbb R^d$, $1\le d\le4$, the centered summands are independent, $|X_i|\le B$, $Z$ is Gaussian with covariance $G\ge\gamma sI_d$, and $\operatorname{cov}(S)=sI_d$, where $s,B>0$ and $0<\gamma\le1$. Put $\tau=C_0B$, with $C_0$ from that supplier, and let $\Phi_s$ be the CDF of $N(0,s)$. There are constants $c_\gamma>0$ and $C_\gamma<\infty$, independent of the summand laws, $m,d,s,B$, with the following properties.

For $1\le j\le d$, let $H_j(x',y)$ be the conditional CDF of $S_j$ given $S_{<j}=x'\in\mathbb R^{j-1}$ obtained by dividing the joint prefix density by its marginal density. These densities are strictly positive, so this defines a probability kernel at every $x'$, including prefixes of probability zero. Its quantile transport
$$T_j(x',z)=H_j(x',\cdot)^{-1}(\Phi_s(z))$$
is jointly Borel measurable and takes a fresh $N(0,s)$ variable to that conditional law. If $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$, then, with $y=T_j(x',z)$,
$$|y-z|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|x'|^2+y^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|x'|+|y|\le c_\gamma s/\tau,$$
and also
$$|T_j(x',z)-z|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|x'|^2+z^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|x'|+|z|\le c_\gamma s/\tau.$$
For $j=1$, the prefix is empty and its norm is zero. The resulting successive coordinate transport $R$ sends $N_d(0,sI_d)$ to the law of $S$ and satisfies
$$|R(g)-g|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|R(g)|^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|R(g)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau.$$

If $d=2a$ with $a\le2$, write $S=(P,D)$ with $P,D\in\mathbb R^a$. The last $a$ successive conditional transports give a jointly measurable $T_p$ taking a fresh $E\sim N_a(0,sI_a)$ to the conditional law of $D$ given $P=p$, and
$$|T_p(e)-e|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|p|^2+|T_p(e)|^2}{s}\right)$$
when $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$ and $|p|,|T_p(e)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau$. The Gaussian reference bridge $E$ is independent of its Gaussian parent.

There is also the following scalar unequal-variance form. Let $L,R$ be independent centered scalar sums of independent variables bounded by $B$ and independent Gaussian terms, with variances $V_L,V_R\in[s/2,s]$, and with Gaussian component variances at least $\gamma V_L,\gamma V_R$, respectively. Put
$$W=V_L+V_R,\qquad w=V_L/W,\qquad v=V_LV_R/W,\qquad P=L+R,\qquad D=L-wP.$$
Then $W\in[s,2s]$, $w\in[1/3,2/3]$, $v\in[s/4,s/2]$. There is a jointly measurable transport taking a fresh $N(0,v)$ variable to $D$ conditional on $P=p$ with
$$|T_p(e)-e|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{p^2+T_p(e)^2}{s}\right)$$
when $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$ and $|p|,|T_p(e)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau$. The corresponding root transport from $N(0,W)$ to $P$ obeys the analogous bound with $|P|^2/s$. The reconstructed children are $L=wP+D$ and $R=(1-w)P-D$.

All these maps are jointly measurable in an additional measurable parameter whenever, on each fixed finite row length, the bounded input laws are probability kernels, their Gaussian covariance and $s$ are measurable functions, and the displayed hypotheses hold parameterwise. This includes countable arrays with different row lengths. No claim here asserts the conditional estimates for raw bounded laws without a positive Gaussian component.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The centered independent Gaussian anchored sum and its parameters as in the Statement; vector norms are Euclidean, and all constants below depend only on $\gamma$.

[A1] AC is assumed and inherited by the Gaussian suppliers. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[F1] The sum has an analytic cumulant with $|K_{uvv}(z)|\le\tau s|u||v|^2$, and every real tilt retains an independent Gaussian component with covariance at least $\gamma sI$. Each coordinate prefix has the same properties. ([[lem-gaussian-anchored-sums-have-cumulant-and-fourier-bounds]])

[F2] Every tilted density is positive and continuously differentiable, has supremum at most $(2\pi\gamma s)^{-d/2}$, and on the small tilt and moderate deviation region has its Gaussian density times $\exp(O_\gamma((\tau/\sqrt s)(1+r^3)))$. Tilted covariance lies between $7sI/8$ and $9sI/8$. The assertions hold in each prefix's coordinates. ([[lem-gaussian-anchored-sum-density-moderate-deviation-bound]])

[F3] Positive definite Gaussian laws have their positive quadratic-form densities, and the standard normal CDF is continuous, strictly increasing, with limits zero and one. ([[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]], [[lem-standard-normal-cdf-is-continuous-and-strictly-increasing]])

[F4] Nonnegative product integration and dominated convergence apply to the integrals below. ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]])

[F5] Integrating a nonnegative product-measurable function against a finite or uniformly sigma-finite kernel gives a measurable function, and finite products of probability kernels are probability kernels. ([[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]], [[lem-finite-products-of-probability-kernels]])

[F6] Integration of derivatives along real line segments gives the corresponding norm and Lipschitz bounds; Euclidean Cauchy sequences converge. ([[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]], [[thm-euclidean-space-complete]])

[F7] The rationals are countable and dense in the reals. ([[thm-rationals-countable]], [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]])

## Proof

1.1 Work with a fixed prefix of length $j\le4$ and write its dimension as $d$ during the proof. Its law satisfies [F1]–[F2]. Set $\sigma=\sqrt s$, $\epsilon=\tau/\sigma$, and normalize coordinates by $\sigma$. Its cumulant $f$ has mean zero, covariance $I$, and third derivatives bounded by $\epsilon|u||v|^2$. Polarization and [F6], integrating along a real segment, give $\|f''(a)-I\|\le\epsilon|a|$ and $|f'(a)-a|\le\epsilon|a|^2/2$. Fix a prefix $x'$, put $b=x'/\sigma$, $\delta=|b|$, and assume $\epsilon\delta$ sufficiently small. The map $a'\mapsto b-(\nabla'f(a',0)-a')$ sends $|a'|\le2\delta$ into itself and has Lipschitz constant at most $2\epsilon\delta<1/2$. Its iterates from zero have geometrically decreasing consecutive distances, hence converge by [F6] to a solution of $\nabla'f(a',0)=b$ with $|a'|\le2\delta$. For the empty prefix use $a'=0$. Put $a=(a',0)$ and let $y_0=\sigma\partial_df(a)$ be the physical last mean under this prefix tilt. The last mixed covariance row at zero vanishes; integrating its Hessian deviation yields $|y_0|\le C\tau\delta^2$. The physical tilt parameter is $h=a/\sigma$, so $\tau|h|\le2\epsilon\delta$ can be kept below $1/8$. [A1, F1, F2, F6, given, construct]

1.2 Let $p,p'$ be the joint and prefix densities. The Gaussian convolution representations in [F2] and [F4] give $\int_{\mathbb R}p(x',y)\,dy=p'(x')$ at every $x'$: integrate the Gaussian joint density over its last coordinate and then integrate the bounded-summand law. Both densities are everywhere positive. Thus $p(x',y)/p'(x')$ defines a probability density for each $x'$ and, by integration, a version of the conditional kernel. Denote tilted densities by $\bar p,\bar p'$. Since $h_d=0$, their exponential factors cancel exactly, and the density $v$ of $S_d-y_0$ conditional on $S'=x'$ is $v(u)=p(x',u+y_0)/p'(x')=\bar p(x',u+y_0)/\bar p'(x')$. The centered tilted covariance $C$ satisfies $\|C/s-I\|\le C\epsilon\delta$ by step 1.1. Apply [F2] to its full density at $(0,u)$ and prefix density at zero. The ratio of the matching Gaussian densities is a centered normal density with variance $\det C/\det C'=1/(C^{-1})_{dd}=s(1+O(\epsilon\delta))$; the determinant identity follows by eliminating the off-diagonal blocks in $C$. Consequently
$$\left|\log\frac{v(u)}{\phi_s(u)}\right|\le C\epsilon\left(1+\delta\left(1+\frac{u^2}{s}\right)+\frac{|u|^3}{s^{3/2}}\right)$$
for $|u|\le c s/\tau$. Here $\phi_s$ is the density of $N(0,s)$, and the small constants also ensure all [F2] moderate bounds for the full centered tilt. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

1.3 In standardized units set $g(t)=\sigma v(\sigma t)$ and let $\phi$ be the standard normal density. Step 1.2 implies, on $|t|\le c/\epsilon$, $|\log(g(t)/\phi(t))|\le C\epsilon(1+\delta+\delta t^2+|t|^3)$ and hence $c_1e^{-C_1t^2}\le g(t)\le C_1e^{-c_1t^2}$ after reducing $\epsilon$ and $\epsilon\delta$. There is also a global bound $g(t)\le C\exp[-c\min(t^2,|t|/\epsilon)]$. Indeed the standardized prefix-tilted law has prefix density at its mean bounded below by a positive constant by [F2]. Tilt its centered full law further by $q e_d$, where $|q|\le c/\epsilon$. Its full density is bounded above by a constant by the global part of [F2], while integration of its bounded Hessian gives a centered log mgf at most $Cq^2$. The density tilt identity therefore gives $g(t)\le C e^{Cq^2-qt}$ at every real $t$. Choosing $q=\operatorname{sign}(t)\min(|t|/(4C),c/(2\epsilon))$ proves the bound. The combined real tilt remains in a fixed smaller analytic ball, where the Hessian bound from step 1.1 applies; the global density bound in [F2] itself permits every real tilt. [F1, F2, F3, F6, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.1 We next convert the density estimate into a CDF displacement without a coupling theorem. Write $R(t)=\epsilon(1+\delta+\delta t+t^2)$ for $t\ge0$. Choose a fixed large $T\ge10$ and then a sufficiently large fixed $K$. Put $r(t)=KR(t)$ and $b=c_0/\epsilon$, with fixed $c_0$ sufficiently small. Reduce the allowed bounds on $\epsilon$ and $\epsilon\delta$ so that for $T/2\le t\le2b$ one has $0\le r(t)\le t/8$ and $0\le r'(t)\le1/2$; this is possible because $R'(t)\le2R(t)/t$ for $t\ge1$ and $r(t)/t\le C K\epsilon(1+\delta+t)$. Also choose $3b$ within the moderate interval of step 1.3. For $t\ge T$, the maps $f_\pm(t)=t\pm r(t)$ are increasing and their arguments are comparable with $t$. Since $(\log\phi)'(t)=-t$, step 1.3 bounds the logarithmic density error at either perturbed argument by $C tR(t)$, whereas the Gaussian log-density changes by at least a fixed positive multiple of $t r(t)$ in the favorable direction. The log Jacobians are at most $r'(t)$ and at least $-2r'(t)$, respectively. Since $r'(t)\le2r(t)/t$, first taking $T$ large and then $K$ large gives $g(f_+(t))f_+'(t)\le\phi(t)$ and $g(f_-(t))f_-'(t)\ge\phi(t)$. These comparisons follow by adding the three logarithmic contributions; the Jacobian contribution divided by $t r(t)$ is at most $4/t^2$, and the density-error contribution is at most $C/K$. [F3, step 1.3, algebra, choose]

2.2 The inverse equations and monotonicity of $r$ imply $f_+^{-1}(z)\ge z-r(z)$ and $f_-^{-1}(z)\le z+r(2z)$ in the range below. Substituting $u=f_+(t)$ and $u=f_-(t)$ in the inequalities of step 2.1 gives, for $2T\le z\le b$,
$$\int_z^b g(u)\,du\le\int_{z-r(z)}^\infty\phi(u)\,du,\qquad \int_z^b g(u)\,du\ge\int_{z+r(2z)}^b\phi(u)\,du.$$
Only a smaller range $z\le c_1/\epsilon$, with $c_1\ll c_0$, will be retained, so the lower integral has its endpoints in the stated order. The global tail estimate in step 1.3 and the Gaussian tail give $\int_b^\infty g+\int_b^\infty\phi\le C e^{-c b^2}$: split the first integral at a constant multiple of $1/\epsilon$ and integrate the Gaussian and exponential parts. Enlarge the shifts in the displayed inequalities to $3r(2z)$. Each extra Gaussian interval has mass at least $cR(z)e^{-Cz^2}\ge c\epsilon e^{-Cz^2}$. Choose $c_1$ so small that $C c_1^2<c c_0^2/2$. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, uniformly for $2T\le z\le c_1/\epsilon$, that interval mass exceeds the discarded tail, since $\epsilon^{-1}\exp(-(c c_0^2-Cc_1^2)/\epsilon^2)\to0$. Thus the full tails have the corresponding inequalities with shift $C R(z)$; here $R(2z)\le4R(z)$. Reflecting $g,\phi$ proves the negative-tail version as well. [F3, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra, choose]

2.3 At $z=2T$ step 2.2 bounds the tail-probability difference by $C R(2T)$. For $|z|\le2T$, step 1.3 bounds the density-ratio error by $C a$, where $a=\epsilon(1+\delta)$; integrating over this fixed interval gives a CDF difference at most $C a$. The Gaussian density is bounded below by a fixed positive constant on $[-2T-1,2T+1]$, so a shift of length $C a$ in either direction dominates that difference, after reducing the allowed bound on $a$ to keep the shift within this compact interval. Since $R(|z|)\ge a$, this proves together with step 2.2, for the standardized conditional CDF $F_g$,
$$\Phi(z-C R(|z|))\le F_g(z)\le\Phi(z+C R(|z|))\qquad(|z|\le c/\epsilon).$$
All constant choices are finite and made in the indicated order; reducing the common cutoff enforces every smallness requirement. Returning to physical units, the CDF $F_v$ of the centered conditional coordinate satisfies $\Phi_s(u-\rho(u))\le F_v(u)\le\Phi_s(u+\rho(u))$, where $\rho(u)=C\tau(1+\delta(1+|u|/\sigma)+u^2/s)$. [F3, step 1.3, step 2.2, algebra, choose]

3.1 Every conditional density is positive and continuous by step 1.2, so its CDF is continuous, strictly increasing and has limits zero and one. Its inverse on $(0,1)$ is therefore unique. For a fresh $N(0,s)$ variable $Z$, [F3] implies that $\Phi_s(Z)$ is uniform: for $0<u<1$, the event $\Phi_s(Z)\le u$ is $Z\le\Phi_s^{-1}(u)$, of probability $u$. Thus the inverse-CDF map has the asserted conditional law. If $Y=T_j(x',Z)$ and $U=Y-y_0$, then $F_v(U)=\Phi_s(Z)$. Step 2.3 and strict monotonicity imply $|U-Z|\le\rho(U)$ whenever $U$ is moderate. Step 1.1 gives $|y_0|/\sigma\le C\epsilon\delta^2\le Cc\delta$, so $|x'|+|Y|\le c s/\tau$ implies the required moderate bounds on $U$ and $\delta$. The inequalities $2\delta|U|/\sigma\le\delta^2+U^2/s$ and $\delta\le1+\delta^2$ now give $|Y-Z|\le C\tau(1+(|x'|^2+Y^2)/s)$. [F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.3, algebra]

3.2 The bound in Gaussian rather than target values follows by bracketing, not by substituting $Z$ for $Y$ in step 3.1. In standardized units fix a Gaussian coordinate $z$ and put $A=1+\delta^2+z^2$, $L=K_1\epsilon A$, with fixed large $K_1$. If $\epsilon\delta$ and $\epsilon|z|$ are small enough, $z\pm L$ remain in the moderate region and the standardized version of $\rho(z\pm L)$ is at most $L/2$. Indeed $\rho(t)\le C\epsilon(1+\delta^2+t^2)$ and $(z\pm L)^2\le2z^2+2L^2$; the extra $C\epsilon L^2$ is absorbed into $L$ because $\epsilon^2 A$ is small. Step 2.3 therefore gives $F_g(z-L)<\Phi(z)<F_g(z+L)$, so its inverse at $\Phi(z)$ lies in $[z-L,z+L]$. Adding the shift $y_0$ from step 1.1 and restoring units gives $|T_j(x',Z)-Z|\le C\tau(1+(|x'|^2+Z^2)/s)$ under the stated Gaussian-value cutoff. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.3, algebra, choose]

4.1 The maps just constructed are jointly measurable, also under the additional parameter in the Statement. On each fixed row length the product of the bounded input-law kernels exists by [F5]. The Gaussian density is jointly Borel in its positive definite covariance and its argument: its determinant and inverse are continuous functions of the matrix entries by their polynomial and cofactor formulas. Consequently $p_\theta(x)=\int q_{G_\theta}(x-\sum_i t_i)\,\bigotimes_i K_i(\theta,dt_i)$ is jointly measurable by [F5], as are the prefix densities, their positive ratios and their CDF integrals. Lebesgue integration here uses its common exhaustion by bounded intervals. The conditional inverse can be written $\inf\{r\in\mathbb Q:H_{j,\theta}(x',r)\ge u\}$; by [F7] this equals the continuous strictly increasing inverse and is jointly measurable, since strict sublevel sets are countable unions of measurable sets indexed by $r\in\mathbb Q$. Compose with the continuous $\Phi_s(z)=\Phi(z/\sqrt s)$. Different finite row lengths are handled on their countable measurable disjoint union. This constructs the kernel versions explicitly at every prefix. [F3, F5, F7, step 1.2, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 Starting with independent Gaussian coordinates of variance $s$, apply the conditional maps successively to coordinates $1,\ldots,d$. Conditional integration of the densities in step 1.2 shows inductively that the first $j$ constructed coordinates have density $p_j$; their joint density is the product of the successive density ratios, which telescopes to $p_j$. The full map $R$ therefore has the law of $S$. On $|R(g)|\le c s/\tau$, every coordinate and prefix meets the target-value cutoff in step 3.1 after reducing $c$ by a fixed factor. Summing at most four coordinate bounds gives $|R(g)-g|\le C\tau(1+|R(g)|^2/s)$. For $S=(P,D)$ apply only its last $a$ conditional maps with the specified prefix $P=p$ and fresh independent Gaussian coordinates; the same telescoping gives the conditional law of $D$ and the same coordinate estimates give $|T_p(e)-e|\le C\tau(1+(|p|^2+|T_p(e)|^2)/s)$. Separate bounds on the two norms imply the joint cutoff by reducing $c$. The Gaussian reference has covariance $sI$, so its parent and bridge coordinate blocks are independent by the product Gaussian density in [F3]. Joint measurability follows by composing the maps of step 4.1. [F3, F4, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

5.1 For the scalar extension put $a=\sqrt{s/W}$, $b=\sqrt{s/v}$ and $Q=(aP,bD)$. Independence gives $\operatorname{Var}(P)=W$, $\operatorname{Cov}(P,D)=V_L-wW=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(D)=V_LV_R/W=v$, hence $\operatorname{cov}(Q)=sI_2$. The stated ranges follow from $V_L,V_R\in[s/2,s]$; the function $uv/(u+v)$ is increasing in either positive argument, giving $v\in[s/4,s/2]$. Thus $a\in[1/\sqrt2,1]$, $b\in[\sqrt2,2]$ and $w\in[1/3,2/3]$. A bounded left increment $X$ contributes $(aX,b(1-w)X)$ to $Q$, whose norm is at most $2B$; a bounded right increment contributes $(aX,-bwX)$ with the same bound. The joint Gaussian component is obtained from independent child Gaussians by the same linear map. Since their variances are at least $\gamma V_L,\gamma V_R$, its covariance, by congruence, is at least $\gamma\operatorname{cov}(Q)=\gamma sI_2$. Therefore $Q$ satisfies the original hypotheses with bound $2B$ and parameter $2\tau$. Apply step 4.2 conditionally on $aP=ap$, feeding $be\sim N(0,s)$, and divide the output by $b$. The uniform bounds on $a,b$ convert its estimate and its cutoffs into the asserted scalar bridge bound after changing $c_\gamma,C_\gamma$ by fixed factors. Applying the scalar root construction to $aP$ and rescaling gives the root bound. Finally $D=L-wP$ rearranges to the two stated child formulas. Every coefficient is a continuous function of the positive variances, so the parameter measurability in step 4.1 is preserved. All conclusions follow. [F1, F3, step 4.1, step 4.2, algebra] ∎

manifest_row.statement:
Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[lem-gaussian-anchored-sums-have-cumulant-and-fourier-bounds]]: $S=Z+\sum_{i=1}^mX_i\in\mathbb R^d$, $1\le d\le4$, the centered summands are independent, $|X_i|\le B$, $Z$ is Gaussian with covariance $G\ge\gamma sI_d$, and $\operatorname{cov}(S)=sI_d$, where $s,B>0$ and $0<\gamma\le1$. Put $\tau=C_0B$, with $C_0$ from that supplier, and let $\Phi_s$ be the CDF of $N(0,s)$. There are constants $c_\gamma>0$ and $C_\gamma<\infty$, independent of the summand laws, $m,d,s,B$, with the following properties.

For $1\le j\le d$, let $H_j(x',y)$ be the conditional CDF of $S_j$ given $S_{<j}=x'\in\mathbb R^{j-1}$ obtained by dividing the joint prefix density by its marginal density. These densities are strictly positive, so this defines a probability kernel at every $x'$, including prefixes of probability zero. Its quantile transport
$$T_j(x',z)=H_j(x',\cdot)^{-1}(\Phi_s(z))$$
is jointly Borel measurable and takes a fresh $N(0,s)$ variable to that conditional law. If $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$, then, with $y=T_j(x',z)$,
$$|y-z|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|x'|^2+y^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|x'|+|y|\le c_\gamma s/\tau,$$
and also
$$|T_j(x',z)-z|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|x'|^2+z^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|x'|+|z|\le c_\gamma s/\tau.$$
For $j=1$, the prefix is empty and its norm is zero. The resulting successive coordinate transport $R$ sends $N_d(0,sI_d)$ to the law of $S$ and satisfies
$$|R(g)-g|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|R(g)|^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|R(g)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau.$$

If $d=2a$ with $a\le2$, write $S=(P,D)$ with $P,D\in\mathbb R^a$. The last $a$ successive conditional transports give a jointly measurable $T_p$ taking a fresh $E\sim N_a(0,sI_a)$ to the conditional law of $D$ given $P=p$, and
$$|T_p(e)-e|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|p|^2+|T_p(e)|^2}{s}\right)$$
when $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$ and $|p|,|T_p(e)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau$. The Gaussian reference bridge $E$ is independent of its Gaussian parent.

There is also the following scalar unequal-variance form. Let $L,R$ be independent centered scalar sums of independent variables bounded by $B$ and independent Gaussian terms, with variances $V_L,V_R\in[s/2,s]$, and with Gaussian component variances at least $\gamma V_L,\gamma V_R$, respectively. Put
$$W=V_L+V_R,\qquad w=V_L/W,\qquad v=V_LV_R/W,\qquad P=L+R,\qquad D=L-wP.$$
Then $W\in[s,2s]$, $w\in[1/3,2/3]$, $v\in[s/4,s/2]$. There is a jointly measurable transport taking a fresh $N(0,v)$ variable to $D$ conditional on $P=p$ with
$$|T_p(e)-e|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{p^2+T_p(e)^2}{s}\right)$$
when $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$ and $|p|,|T_p(e)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau$. The corresponding root transport from $N(0,W)$ to $P$ obeys the analogous bound with $|P|^2/s$. The reconstructed children are $L=wP+D$ and $R=(1-w)P-D$.

All these maps are jointly measurable in an additional measurable parameter whenever, on each fixed finite row length, the bounded input laws are probability kernels, their Gaussian covariance and $s$ are measurable functions, and the displayed hypotheses hold parameterwise. This includes countable arrays with different row lengths. No claim here asserts the conditional estimates for raw bounded laws without a positive Gaussian component.
